title: Writing your own smart pointer
objectives: Implement a minimal unique pointer and a reference-counted pointer.

screens.title: Six steps, one counter
screens.prose: A shared pointer is built in steps. Slide through six: `a` is made, then copied twice, then the three go out of scope in turn.
screens.question: How many times does `new` run across these six steps?

widget.accept: 2: the object and the counter, both at step 1

hints.text: Look at which steps add a new box.
Only the first step adds boxes.
A copy adds an arrow, not a box.

feedback.correct: Twice: one for the object and one for the counter, both in step 1.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Count the boxes that appear, not the arrows.

byKey.three: You counted a new counter for each copy. A copy shares the counter that already exists.

explain.text: Step 1 allocates the object and the counter. Each copy adds an arrow to both and one to the count, with no new allocation. The last owner frees both.

screens.title: Who holds the count
screens.prose: After `a`, `b = a` and `c = b`, three pointers share one object.
screens.question: How many counters exist on the heap?

hints.text: Follow the arrows from `a`, `b` and `c` to the counter.
They all end at the same box.
One counter, shared.

feedback.correct: One counter, shared by all three.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Count the counter boxes in the picture.

byKey.three: You gave each pointer its own count. If each kept its own, no pointer would know when the others had gone. One counter is shared.

explain.text: The counter lives on the heap beside the object, so every owner can reach it. The last one to subtract sees zero and frees both.

screens.title: Write the unique pointer
screens.prose: A unique pointer owns one object or nothing. Write the destructor, delete copying, write the two moves, and finish `release()` and `reset()`.

lines: { UniquePtr<Tracked> p(new Tracked(5)); }   // Tracked::live is 0 after
UniquePtr<Tracked> q = p;               // does not compile
UniquePtr<Tracked> q = std::move(p);    // p is now empty

hints.text: The destructor is `delete ptr_;`, and a null pointer is safe to delete.
A move takes the pointer and sets the source's to null.
`release()` returns the pointer and nulls it. `reset(p)` deletes the old one, then owns `p`.

feedback.correct: One owner at a time, and the object is deleted exactly once.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. A live count above 0 is a leak, and a negative count is a double delete.

byKey.compile: The compiler stopped. Check the deleted copy members and the move signatures.

explain.text: Deleting the copy members makes ownership single. The move hands it over and nulls the source, so exactly one destructor frees the object.

screens.title: Why two pointers wide
screens.prose: On a desk machine `sizeof(std::unique_ptr<int>)` is one pointer and `sizeof(std::shared_ptr<int>)` is two. Here that is 4 and 8 bytes.
screens.question: Why is the shared one two pointers wide?

options.text: It also points at the counter block

options.why: A count inside each pointer would not be shared between copies.
The deleter lives in the counter block, not in each pointer.
Padding does not double a pointer.

hints.text: What must every owner be able to reach?
A count that all owners share.
One pointer for the object and one for the counter.

feedback.correct: The second pointer leads to the shared counter block.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Think of what all the copies must share.

byKey.inside: You put the count in each pointer. A count inside each pointer would not be shared between copies.
byKey.deleter: The deleter lives in the counter block, not in each pointer.
byKey.align: Padding does not double a pointer.

explain.text: One pointer reaches the object and one reaches the counter block. The unique pointer needs only the first.

screens.title: Copy assignment, in order
screens.prose: Order the lines of `SharedPtr`'s copy assignment. One line is a tempting order that breaks `a = a`.
screens.question: Put the lines in order, and leave the flawed one out.

lines.text: drop this pointer's own count first, then add one to `other`'s
lines.why: For `a = a` the count falls to zero and the object is deleted. Then you add to a freed counter.

lines.text: drop this pointer's own count: subtract one, and at zero delete the object and the counter

hints.text: Make sure the new object stays alive while the old one is released.
Take your new share before you give up the old one.
Add to `other`, subtract from yourself, then copy the pointers.

feedback.correct: Add first, subtract second, copy third: `a = a` stays safe.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Think about `a = a`.

byKey.d1: You dropped first. For `a = a` the count falls to zero and the object is deleted, then you add to a freed counter.

explain.text: Adding first means `a = a` never lets the count reach zero. Dropping first could free the object you are about to share.

screens.prose: The constructor from a raw pointer starts a counter at 1. Write the copy and move members and the destructor. The last owner deletes the object and the counter.

options.text: Each count reaches zero, so the object is deleted twice: undefined behaviour
The count is 2, so it is deleted once
options.why: You gave the count as 2. Each constructor from a raw pointer starts its own count at 1.
It is freed, twice; not never.

options.text: It is deleted once, because the counters know about each other
options.why: The counters do not know about each other.

Each pointer decrements its own.
Both reach zero, and each then deletes the object.

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Count the counters first.

byKey.two: You gave the count as 2. Each constructor from a raw pointer starts its own count at 1.
byKey.leak: It is freed, twice; not never.
byKey.once: The counters do not know about each other.

explain.text: Each pointer built from the raw one made its own counter, so each deletes the object when its count reaches zero. Make a shared owner with `make_shared`, or copy an existing `shared_ptr`, never from one raw pointer twice.

screens.title: Add before you drop
screens.prose: Your `operator=` adds one to the other count, then drops its own.
screens.question: In `operator=`, why add to the other count before dropping your own?

options.text: `a = a`: the count could fall to zero and free the object before it is taken again
It is faster that way round
The count is atomic and must be changed first
options.why: The real count is atomic, ours is not, and that is unrelated to the order.

hints.text: What happens if both sides are the same pointer?
If you drop first, the count may reach zero.
Then the object is deleted before you copy it.

feedback.correct: Add first keeps the object alive in `a = a`.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Think about `a = a` and the count.

byKey.speed: You thought it saves time. Order makes no speed difference.
byKey.atomic: The real count is atomic, ours is not, and that is unrelated to the order.

explain.text: The next questions an interviewer asks: is it thread safe (the count is atomic, the pointee is not), what is `weak_ptr` (a handle that does not add to the count), and what is `enable_shared_from_this`.

screens.title: Unique or shared
screens.question: What does copying a `shared_ptr` cost that moving one does not?

options.text: An atomic add to the shared count

options.why: A copy shares the existing counter. It allocates nothing.

options.text: Nothing: both are just pointer copies
options.why: Every copy adds one to a shared count, and the add is atomic.

feedback.correct: An atomic add to the count. A move takes the pointers and leaves it alone.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Think about the count.

explain.text: A copy increments the shared count, atomically. A move transfers the two pointers and touches nothing else.

screens.title: A feed handler
screens.prose: A feed handler makes 200,000 messages a second as `std::shared_ptr<Message>(new Message)`. Take an allocation as 50 ns, a round figure.
screens.question: Fill in the three figures.

rows: milliseconds a second the change saves

hints.text: Each message needs an object. How many blocks does `shared_ptr(new T)` make?
The object, and the counter block.
`make_shared` builds both in one block. Then multiply the difference by 50 ns.

feedback.correct: 400,000 and 200,000 allocations, saving 10 ms a second.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Count the blocks a message needs each way.

byKey.r0c1: You may have given the `make_shared` count. `new` gives one allocation for the object and one for the counter.
byKey.r1c1: `make_shared` builds the object and the counter in one block: one allocation a message.
byKey.r2c1: 200,000 allocations at 50 ns is 10,000,000 ns, which is 10 ms.

explain.text: `new` plus the counter is 2 blocks a message, so 400,000 a second. `make_shared` is one, so 200,000, and the 200,000 saved at 50 ns are 10,000,000 ns, 10 ms.

ideas: A smart pointer is a class whose destructor frees what it owns. A unique one deletes copying and moves ownership, leaving the source null.
A shared pointer holds the object pointer and a pointer to a counter block that all owners share. The last owner deletes both.
Add to the other count before dropping your own, so `a = a` is safe. Never build two shared pointers from one raw pointer.

formula.name: The shared count
formula.note: One counter, shared by every owner.

summary.trap: Two shared pointers built from one raw pointer have two counters, so the object is deleted twice.

quiz.question: Which of `release()` and `reset()` deletes the object?

options.why: `release()` gives up ownership and returns the pointer. Nothing is deleted.
`release()` hands the object to the caller, who must delete it.

feedback.generic: Not quite right. One of them gives the pointer away.

explain.text: `release()` returns the raw pointer and stops owning it. `reset()` deletes what it owns.
